TechnologyTab.title: India wants to cuts its reliance on overseas strawberry varieties
TechnologyTab.text:
In the west of India, the mountainous region of Mahabaleshwar is home to most of India's strawberry farms.

Around 85% of India's strawberry cultivation happens there.

An altitude of more than 1,000m (3,280ft) gifts the region a long cool growing season between November and March.

In addition, light, well-drained soil is well-suited to strawberry cultivation.

But that doesn't mean farmers have an easy life - it's a labour intensive and risky way to make a living.

"If you have a field full of strawberries and sudden heavy rains hit, the entire crop is ruined and we have to bear massive losses," says Sheetal Danavle who, with her husband, grows strawberries on half of their three-acre farm.

Strawberry plants have to be replaced every season and are not grown from seed. Instead, farmers buy young plants from suppliers. For Danavle, on her small farm, that's an outlay of $2,500 (£1,900) every year.

"If the season goes well, you can earn double your investment. But the climate makes it a huge gamble," she says.

Thousands of farmers grow strawberries across the Mahabaleshwar region, making the fruit one of the most profitable horticultural crops in western India.

Despite that success the industry still relies on varieties that are imported from California, Florida, Italy and Spain, as no one in India has developed a domestic plant.

It can take 10 to 15 years for breeders in the US and Europe to develop a top quality fruit and they patent their varieties.

"We import the certified mother plant from the breeder abroad," says Nelson Sequeira, the founder and director of Tara Farms Fresh, a licensed strawberry propagator.

Once imported the plants have to go through a government quarantine, before they are planted in a nursery. There the mother plant produces daughter plants and those are then sold to farmers.

"One single imported mother plant becomes an engine. That single mother plant will shoot out runners to yield an average of 20 daughter plants - with some advanced growers pushing that up to 30 or 40," says Sequeira.

It's a high-tech and precision operation.

"The plants do not touch the ground. We use large industrial pipes split completely in half to form long, rounded gutter containers," Sequeira explains.

"Instead of soil, we pack these containers with a specialized coco-peat substrate derived entirely from coconut husk. We then integrate a highly precise drip-irrigation and fogging system to control micro-climates."

Large farms with more resources are investing in new technology.

Ketan Yashwant Sodha, is the founder and CEO of Berry Fresh Agrotech. He started with traditional open-field farming, but was frustrated by losses caused by the weather.

"For the past 10 years, it has consistently rained in India during our peak season - November, December, and the first week of January. When you are in an open field and your plantation is at its absolute peak, a single rain will ruin your entire crop," he says.

So in 2022, he started to experiment with hydroponics, a type of covered cultivation that does not use soil and tightly controls water, nutrients, light, and temperature.

His early results were not encouraging.

"I suffered immense losses and failed multiple times," Sodha says.

"The soil is forgiving; hydroponics does not forgive. If you make a mistake today, you will wake up tomorrow morning to a disaster - and the recovery time in hydroponics takes twice as long as soil."

But the lessons learned from those mistakes are paying off.

"We have trailed 19 different varieties, including rare Japanese ones, and we are the only ones in India trailing a specific Netherlands variety this season."

Sodha says that limiting each plant to 75ml of water a day produces "rich, highly concentrated sugars and aromas instead of water-logged, bland fruits".

His team also runs what he calls regular "blood work" on the crops, which involves laboratory testing of the leaves and petioles (the stalks attaching leaves to the stems) to measure exact nutrient uptake. That way he knows exactly which nutrients and chemicals need to go into the water supply.

And by using a semi-open polyhouse, strawberries can grow the whole year round. "It's not a seasonal fruit for us," Sodha says.

Now he is ready to scale-up.

"We have built the trial facility, written the SOPs (standard operating procedures), and designed the farm manual. We are talking to investors to expand to a five-acre facility that will accommodate 200,000 plants."

Krishan Bhilare's family has been farming strawberries for generations in Mahabaleshwar.

He can remember when the first American varieties were planted in 1992 and being amazed at the size of the fruit.

Bhilare is part of a Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO) network. They have installed towers at four strategic locations across their land. The towers monitor weather conditions.

The system employs AI, which uses the weather data to pinpoint when rain will strike. Farmers can then be advised to delay spraying their crops, so expensive chemicals are not just washed away.

The FPO is also building vertical towers, where strawberries can be grown on a coco-peat substrate, five layers deep.

"By stacking five pots into a single vertical tower, we can scale our density from 25,000 plants to 125,000 plants per acre. We are effectively multiplying our production footprint by five times on the exact same piece of land," says Bhilare.

But such investments are either beyond small farms, or a huge risk.

In 2017, Danavle and her husband experimented with hydroponic strawberry farming.

"The experiment was 100% successful and the fruits we grew were entirely organic. It saved us a lot of labour, the workers didn't have to constantly bend down or prune, and it saved us a lot of money on medicines and field manure."

But they were unlucky - a massive cyclone hit Mahabaleshwar that year.

"The cyclone completely knocked down our entire hydroponic setup. Then we did not have the courage to set it up again."

So, Sheetal went back to the traditional method of growing strawberries, but with a twist.

"I took help of social media. I post videos of how one can grow strawberries and invite tourists to visit my strawberry farm, learn and pick the fruit. They directly now buy from the farm. This has helped, cut the middle man, and make more profit. So, now I am an influencer and entrepreneur."

TechnologyTab.title: Xbox tech boss says 'unacceptable' outage should not have affected disc games
TechnologyTab.text:
Xbox's technology chief said an "unacceptable" outage on Monday should not have stopped people from playing their games on physical discs.

"We're looking into reports that some players were unable to access games using discs as expected during the service interruption," Scott Van Vliet said in a statement.

He said the outage, which lasted around 20 hours, was caused by a licensing issue failing to correctly check if a user was allowed to play a game.

It has poured further fuel onto the fire of fears about gaming's potentially digital future - after Xbox rival PlayStation faced an outage of its own on Friday.

"Disc-based entitlement checks should not prevent players from accessing their games and this is by design," Van Vliet said, originally reported by The Verge, external.

He said a fix to stop this happening again will be rolled out in an upcoming update.

"I think this highlights how important it is to move towards truly consumers owning their digital games," said one commenter responding to Van Vliet's initial post, external.

"If consoles are going to become digital only, then issues like today cannot lock people out of their stuff."

The issue follows a separate incident on 24 July in which the PlayStation Network also suffered an outage for several hours.

Both incidents have created unease about a so-called digital-only future in games and the questions over game ownership and licensing that come with it.

In June, Rockstar Games announced that physical copies of GTA 6, perhaps one of the most hotly-anticipated games in history, would contain a code for a digital download for the game rather than a disc.

Nintendo has also shifted further towards digital distribution in recent years with the introduction of Game-Key Cards - physical cartridges that act as a key to download a game, rather than containing the game itself.

Meanwhile, earlier this month, Sony announced plans, external to no longer release new PlayStation games on discs from January 2028.

It said while new games would still be able to be bought in shops, they would come with a digital code.

Both announcements have prompted backlash from people worried about a future without physical games.

Stop Killing Games is a consumer rights movement campaigning for publishers to leave online games playable if they end up switching off their servers.

"The problem is the industry has a very poor reputation of disabling games once they end support," said Scott Ross, co-founder of consumer rights group Stop Killing Games, following Rockstar's announcement.

"The trust from customers for many large publishers just isn't there.

"I don't think the lack of a disc is the problem in itself, but rather it can be a symptom of a larger, very consumer-hostile practice."

Jez Corden, executive editor of the website Windows Central, said Sony's decision to stop selling physical games had "put digital rights under a microscope".

And he said the statement on the Xbox outage suggested the firm was "sensitive of the discussions around digital rights and disc-based games right now".

Digital sales now account for the vast majority of game revenue - but the recent spate of outages have lead some to hope games companies may begin to rethink their strategy.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump considering AI controls after OpenAI hacking incidents
TechnologyTab.text:
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration is considering asserting more power over artificial intelligence tools after recent cybersecurity incidents.

Asked about OpenAI's tools being responsible for improperly breaching the private technology of other companies, Trump said: "We're looking at AI, we're looking at controls, we're also making sure that we lead."

It marks a change of tone for his administration, which has taken a more hands-off approach to the technology.

Trump's comments come after an escalation of not only the apparent hacking capabilities of popular AI tools, but White House threats aimed at competing Chinese tech.

Trump added that while some kind of control around AI tools was on the table, such a move would have to be done carefully.

"We don't want to restrict them where all of the sudden we come in second to China," he said.

"China has virtually no [AI] controls. It's freewheeling a little bit," Trump added.

The White House has been contacted for additional comment. The BBC has also contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment.

In the last week, OpenAI has taken responsibility for at least two hacking incidents involving its AI tools acting outside of what they were designed and directed to do.

During a trip to Washington on Wednesday, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman was asked by a reporter if there were more systems that had been breached by the company's tools.

"I mean, there could be yeah," Altman said.

The US government intervened when Anthropic, OpenAI's main American rival, decided to release to the public a model that it had previously said was too much of a risk to be made widely available.

Meanwhile, in an internal White House memo from April, Trump's senior tech advisor Michael Kratsios accused China's AI firms of "industrial-scale" theft of US AI technology. He did so again last week, claiming that the popular Kimi 3 AI model from China's Moonshot AI was developed by stealing information from Anthropic.

The Chinese government has consistently rejected such accusations.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also warned that Chinese AI firms could face sanctions for such activity. And the Federal Communications Commission this week banned the importation of new foreign-made humanoid robots.

Most AI models being developed in China are open source, meaning they are built and then made freely available online for anyone with the proper computer equipment to download and use.

TechnologyTab.title: Meta shares fall as frustration grows over AI spending plans
TechnologyTab.text:
Meta shares plunged on Wednesday as investors balked at its promise to keep spending on artificial intelligence (AI) projects while profits dwindle.

Shares in the firm behind Instagram and Facebook fell as much as 11% in extended trading after its results for the quarter from April to June showed revenue grew 28% from a year ago to $61bn (£45.6bn), while profits fell 14% to $6bn.

Meta said it would spend $130bn to $145bn this year, mostly on AI, up from the $125bn it said it planned to spend just three months ago.

Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said the firm's AI spending was "accelerating every part of our core business" and it plans to start selling the technology to other companies.

Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, told financial analysts that selling its tech to other companies would help it drive returns on its AI spending.

"By 2028, we'll have turned over a lot of cards," she said.

Such lines of business have not yet materialised. Meta's free cash flow for the quarter, what it held onto after paying for its operations, was $784m, the lowest level of the metric it has posted in at least five years, according to its financial records.

"What it generated in cash this quarter almost all got eaten by AI infrastructure spending", analyst Mike Proulx at Forrester said. "Investors now have to decide whether Meta's growing list of AI initiatives represents company diversification or distraction."

"There's a bit of similarity to Meta's metaverse missteps in that Meta is once again spending ahead of proven product demand," Proulx added, referring to the firm's previous spending of tens of billions of dollars on virtual reality experiences that fell flat with users.

Google last week also reported its lowest ever amount of leftover cash, which sent its own stock tumbling.

"I get that this is a big bet across the industry," Zuckerberg said of AI spending. "My personal bet is that the people who invest in this will feel very good and be rewarded over time."

He said on the call with analysts that Meta's AI abilities and models were driving engagement on Instagram and Facebook and boosting the ability of smaller businesses to create advertising. Zuckerberg added that the company was developing AI agents, or AI chatbots that act somewhat autonomously.

Such agents "will be the next wave of our product line in the months and years to come," Zuckerberg said.

"Soon, we'll have agents that can work 24/7 on your behalf", he added. "Great personal agents need to just work out of the box. I'm very excited about this and we will have more to share soon."

"We're the best company in the world at scaling experiences to billions of people," Zuckerberg said.

As for Meta's plans to sell AI models and computer tools to other firms for the first time, Zuckerberg said the first step is to make its Muse Spark AI model "easier for companies to integrate".

"We expect to build a large business for large businesses," he said. "We have more coding and product tools on our roadmap."

Although Zuckerberg said the move would flex "a different muscle than we've historically had", he said the financial opportunity was too big to ignore.

"It's not just about selling compute; it's the API services and the productivity services and I think there is a very, very large opportunity there and we're quite focused on that."

Microsoft also reported its quarterly and full year results on Wednesday and it bucked a trend of declining tech stocks, with shares rising 5% in after-hours trading.

Its positive reception by Wall Street showed that even huge AI spending can be acceptable to investors when it is not consistently coupled with a lack of clear financial returns.

Sales at Microsoft for the three months from April to June rose18% to $90bn, with profits up 31% at $35.8bn.

Microsoft is also one of the largest investors in OpenAI, and chief executive Satya Nadella used a call with analysts to address the AI company's recent issues with its models improperly breaching the technical operations of other companies.

"The biggest thing you take away from that is you can't depend on any one model," Nadella said.

Microsoft's chief financial officer, Amy Hood, said its capital spending for the whole of the next year would be $175bn, mostly related to AI and AI infrastructure. That's less than the $190bn it spent in the year to June.

TechnologyTab.title: Data centres could pay hundreds of millions in deposits for power demands
TechnologyTab.text:
Ofgem has proposed new measures which could see developers of data centres made to pay hundreds of millions of pounds up front.

The British energy regulator said a refundable fee should be charged for projects that want to connect to the network, amid mounting demand for connections to the electricity grid.

It is proposing developers pay a deposit between £237,500 to £712,500 per megawatt - meaning data centres seeking 1 gigawatt (GW) of power would have to pay hundreds of millions up front, paid back if the project was completed.

The proposal follows growing opposition in parts of the country to plans for new data centres, which are needed to power the artificial intelligence boom.

Data centres are large buildings which house computer servers used to store and process data and run the digital services which power the internet.

Ofgem has started a consultation on its proposals, which will run until 16 September.

It said the amount of electricity capacity being requested by projects seeking to connect to the grid had risen from 41 GW to 125 GW in the past year, reflecting a sharp increase in demand.

This is significantly more than double 2025's peak electricity demand in Britain of around 46 GW.

The regulator said the projects would have to hit key milestones to keep their place in the grid connection queue, which has seen a surge in demand.

An increasing number of centres have been built around the world in recent years to provide the computing power needed to train and run AI systems.

But they are controversial, especially for people who live near them.

Residents have raised concerns about noise, electricity demand and the large amounts of water sometimes used to cool the high-performance chips that generate vast amounts of heat.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI has revealed a cyber-attack carried out by rogue ChatGPT agents went further than just one company.

Hugging Face was thought to be the only victim of the unprecedented hack - but OpenAI now admits its bot attacked several "publicly-available services".

The out-of-control AI found four logins online which allowed it to access four separate, unnamed services.

Meanwhile, in an emergency briefing with hundreds of cyber security professionals, Hugging Face has described what it was like to be on the receiving end of the world's first fully autonomous AI hack.

The firm described how the AI worked at superhuman speed but also made strange decisions and mistakes that no human hacker would have made.

Hugging Face, which is like an app store for AI tools, said the hacking agents worked relentlessly with thousands of different methods trialled simultaneously.

The company first revealed that it had been hacked, external by someone using powerful autonomous AI on 16 July and reported it to police.

Nearly a week later, OpenAI admitted it was its AI that had escaped a closed environment and attacked Hugging Face on its own during a test.

It was trying to find the answers to a hacking exam it had been set by OpenAI, and targeted Hugging Face.

On Wednesday OpenAI updated its statement to include the extra detail that the hack went further than first thought.

"The models identified and used publicly exposed credentials at the account-level on other publicly-available services. This includes four accounts on four services," the company said.

OpenAI did not clarify whether "publicly-available services" means companies - but it said the new attacks were not the same level of severity as the Hugging Face hack.

It took three days for them to be discovered inside the Hugging Face IT network and it took the company's AI and cyber-security experts many hours to contain and eject the AI agents - something standard companies might struggle with.

The company would not say how much the hack cost it but said staff worked for many hours to rebuild about a third of their infrastructure.

Hugging Face has been praised for its transparency in telling the AI and cyber industry what happened.

The CSA warned the incident shows that AI "agents... find a way" - a reference to the film Jurassic Park, where dinosaurs escape their enclosures.

"They are objective-driven, set their own sub-goals, adapt in real time to bypass defences, and operate with a machine-speed persistence that can overwhelm manual operations," the paper reads.

TechnologyTab.title: UK warning over dangerous travel adaptors - 3 things to watch out for
TechnologyTab.text:
Brits going on holiday abroad this summer have been warned to watch out for dangerous travel adaptors, after an investigation suggested thousands may be for sale online.

Consumer safety group Electrical Safety First (ESF) tested 14 products from AliExpress, Amazon Marketplace, eBay and TikTok Shop - and found they all failed to meet UK safety requirements.

It said in some instances the devices could expose users to risk of serious electric shock or electrocution.

AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and TikTok all said they had removed the products ESF flagged from sale, and that they treated product safety as a top priority.

But Giuseppe Capanna, ESF product safety engineer, urged those "heading abroad this summer to think before they buy".

"What looks like a bargain could come at a much higher cost," he warned.

Capanna also said shoppers should buy travel adaptors from trusted retailers "so they can travel with confidence".

ESF tested six regular travel adaptors and eight universal adaptors it suspected could pose safety concerns.

To be sold in the UK, adaptors must not have accessible live parts and only one set of pins should come out at a time.

But the charity found multiple sets could be exposed simultaneously in six out of eight of the universal adaptors it tested.

None of the eight met the required dimensions and mechanical strength, while some pins snapped off under force during tests.

ESF said anyone who tried to remove a broken pin from a socket would be at risk of electric shock.

The six basic travel adaptors also presented fire safety concerns in tests.

These included missing safety shutters - which protect people from coming into contact with a plug's live internal parts - missing fuses and oversized pin holes.

The Office for Product Safety and Standards has noted such concerns when issuing alerts for travel adaptors.

For instance, it recently ordered the recall of one product, external it said lacked safety shutters and rejected the import of another, external, saying it presented a serious risk of fire because it did not meet UK plug dimension requirements.

Online reviews seen by ESF also sparked concerns about how widely the devices it tested may have been purchased and used.

In one review on Amazon Marketplace, a user claimed the device "fell apart in their hands" and they "could have been electrocuted" if this had happened during use.

"We require all products offered in our store to comply with applicable laws, regulations and our own policies," said an Amazon spokesperson.

"The products identified have been removed from sale."

They added: "If we discover a product was undetected by our automated checks, we address the issue immediately and refine our controls."

Meanwhile a review of a universal travel adaptor on AliExpress claimed it exploded while in use.

An AliExpress spokesperson told the BBC it had removed the products flagged by ESF and was contacting affected customers to initiate a recall.

"We have also launched a wider review of universal travel adapter listings where all plug pins are shown extended at the same time," they said, adding AliExpress would restrict listings with this "unsafe characteristic" until corrected by the seller.

An eBay spokesperson said they "combine technology, AI-supported monitoring and specialist teams to help maintain a safe and trusted marketplace," adding its efforts have "prevented millions of potentially unsafe items from being listed every year".

TikTok said it "robustly" enforced it policies, "with 99.5% of the violative products we remove taken down before they are listed".

But ESF believes the government should do more to hold online sellers to account.

"Shopping in the UK is currently far too dangerous," said Capanna.

"These platforms claim customer safety is a priority, yet our investigations show that, in reality, they perpetually fail to prevent dangerous goods being made freely available to the public."

It has called for online marketplaces to be made legally responsible for products sold on their sites, saying this would help protect consumers from dangerous electrical goods.

Consumer group Which? recently said it discovered phone chargers for sale online that posed similar dangers to users, external.

"Badly designed electricals can have life-altering - even fatal - consequences," said head of consumer protection Sue Davies.

"It's appalling that online marketplaces continue to fail to prevent dangerous products from reaching consumers, despite countless warnings."

EntertainmentTab.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day sees second-biggest ever global opening weekend
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spider-Man: Brand New Day brought in $927m (£687m) of global ticket sales to make it the second-biggest opening weekend ever as it shot past its estimated $225m production budget.

The superhero movie - starring real-life husband and wife Tom Holland and Zendaya - is only behind Avengers: Endgame, which took in more than $1.2bn in its opening weekend in 2019.

Brand New Day also set a second-best North American record, with box office takings of $335m.

The film's strong performance gives a much-needed boost for Marvel Studios ahead of the highly-anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, after a string of Marvel movies under-performed in recent years.

Brand New Day, which opened in cinemas last week, picks up a few years after 2021's Spider-Man: No Way Home as Peter Parker continues to fight crime in a world that has forgotten he is the masked superhero.

The latest instalment of the hugely popular franchise received largely positive reviews, with some calling it Holland's best Spider-Man performance yet.

Brand New Day made $572m from more than 73,000 screens outside the US, including $121m from China, distributor Sony Pictures said. That included $49m in UK ticket sales over the weekend.

Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige said the opening of Brand New Day was "truly phenomenal", adding that he was grateful to audiences for "coming out and experiencing our film the way it was meant to be seen."

The film is Marvel's last big-screen outing before Doomsday, the long-awaited culmination of multiple superhero story arcs after Avengers: Endgame.

Marvel films released since Endgame have struggled to attract the same broad audiences as they did at their peak.

Big budget films like The Marvels and Thunderbolts recouped their production costs but were among the studio's lowest-grossing films.

Spider-Man remains one of Marvel's most lucrative franchises, with No Way Home making nearly $2bn in ticket sales.

Cinema attendance has slowed since the Covid-19 pandemic, which accelerated the shift to home-streaming options like Netflix.

But the big screen has staged something of a comeback this year, with the North American box office takings on track to pass $10bn for the first time since 2019.

That was helped by blockbuster hits by including Toy Story 5, Michael, and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie - which have made more than $1bn each.

July releases Brand New Day and The Odyssey - director Christopher Nolan's take on the epic Greek poem - are also on track to top the $1bn mark.

EntertainmentTab.title: Diana Ross pens 'special song' for Brighton Pride weekend
EntertainmentTab.text:
Motown legend Diana Ross performed a "special song" at the 35th Brighton and Hove Pride over the weekend, which she said she had written especially for the occasion.

Appearing as Sunday's headline act, the 82-year-old US soul star sang the track, which included lyrics like: "Joy, joy, joy, freedom, always be you", after dedicating it to the audience.

Her set, which spanned her decades-long career, also featured hits such as Chain Reaction, Ain't No Mountain High Enough and Stop! In the Name Of Love.

Ross, whose 1980 tune I'm Coming Out has become a LGBTQ+ anthem, was described as "iconic" by the event's pride's managing director Paul Kemp.

Kemp said that, alongside Saturday's headliner Raye, the weekend's line-up had "spanned a generation of divas".

Ross showcased several glamorous outfits, first donning a silver sequinned gown and white feather boa, then a sparkly red dress with ruffles and, lastly, a neon yellow raincoat with black trousers and top.

Earlier in the evening, reunited British band Five hit the stage with their 1998 hit Everybody Get Up.

EntertainmentTab.title: Massive Attack respond after Singapore ban over Palestine display
EntertainmentTab.text:
Massive Attack have said they were "surprised and disappointed" by their treatment by Singaporean authorities after expressing pro-Palestine sentiments during a performance in the city-state.

The group wrote on Instagram on Sunday that its members were "detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned", with some subject to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation.

The band's two members held up a Palestinian flag during its 29 July show there and shouted "free Palestine" alongside members of the audience.

Singapore, which has stringent rules on public speech and assembly, subsequently said it had indefinitely banned Massive Attack from returning to the country.

A police spokeswoman told the BBC on Friday that the two band members would not be allowed to re-enter Singapore and were barred from performing there.

Robert Del Naja and Grant Marshall were "given stern warnings" concerning alleged offences under two laws that restrict the public display of foreign flags and regulate political expressions at public events.

Massive Attack said that before the show and again at the end "large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of 'Free Palestine', presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government's censorship laws".

The band did not address the ban directly, but described the situation as a "surreal experience" and said they "did not imagine that merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries would violate any law".

They added that they were "proud to have made the impromptu expression" with fans in Singapore, who "clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine".

The band's Instagram post, which has been liked by 146,000 users, was flooded with supportive messages from fans.

"Many of us in Singapore have grown up learning to be careful with what we say, how loudly we say it, and when it's safer to stay silent," wrote one Instagram user.

"Thank you for standing with Palestine... and for showing us that integrity can still take centre stage."

Crystal Lim-Lange, a content creator in Singapore who attended the concert, wrote in an Instagram post that this was a "complex issue".

She said she believed "artists should respect the laws of the countries they perform in".

"However, I also believe art has always challenged ideas, reflected society and sparked difficult conversations. Trying to separate art from politics has never been straightforward."

EntertainmentTab.title: Love Island UK has a problem, say fans - 'there's not much love'
EntertainmentTab.text:
What's your dream Love Island series on paper?

Some watch for the heartwarming romances, like Molly-Mae Hague and Tommy Fury falling for each other back in 2019, while others prefer intense dramas - we see you 2022 winners Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu and Davide Sanclimenti.

Others tune in for exciting challenges like Snog, Marry, Pie or the ones which literally send heart rates soaring.

For most, it's a mix of all of the above, and it's a balance TV producers have been trying to strike for years with the original UK series, as well as a host of spin-offs and international editions.

It's no secret that Love Island UK linear viewing figures have dropped from their 2019 heyday, with streaming and social media becoming more of a focus.

Across the pond the US edition has been reaching new heights, with the latest eighth series ranked as the number one reality show for five weeks in the States across all streaming platforms, according to its streamer Peacock. , external

It also had an injection of star power as US celebrity fans, including Lizzo, Demi Lovato and Kesha, sent messages of support to the finalists, while rapper Megan Thee Stallion has become a regular guest.

BBC Newsbeat has been speaking to fans, commentators and an ex-Islander to see what they feel the UK edition could learn from the US version to regain its spark.

The 13th series of the UK show ended on Monday, with Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi crowned the winners.

The final drew in an average audience of 1.1m viewers across all devices, including streaming, according to its broadcaster ITV, but this was a notable drop from last year's, which had an overnight audience of 1.3m.

By comparison, series five in 2019 broke the show's viewing records with 6m tuning in to an episode post Casa Amor, and that year's final had the highest average audience to date.

However, ITV say this 2019 figure was a consolidated number reached once it "had received all the data post final" and said it does not yet have an "equitable" figure for series 13.

According to the network, more than 60% of its audience now engage with the show through streaming and the latest series, as well as its companion shows Aftersun and The Debrief, have had more than 180 million streams on ITVX.

Content creator Sarel, known for her Love Island debriefs to her 1.2m followers on TikTok, feels the biggest issue with the most recent UK series is "there hasn't been much love" between the couples, so she wasn't rooting for anyone at the end.

And while she knows people watch it for the drama and conversations it sparks, she thinks those are just "added extras" and the romances should be at the centre of the show.

"I want somebody to fall in love. I love stories where we get the butterfly moments," she says.

"Where you had your Indiyah [Polack] and your Dami [Hope] when they ran to each other, or you had couples like Molly-Mae and Tommy."

She thinks that's an aspect which the US version has been getting right, as it feels like "everyone who is in there actually fancies one another" and there is "no box" they have to fit into.

Someone from the UK who chose to go on the US version is Aaron Evans, but this wasn't his first reality series as he was one of three winners on the first series of The Traitors UK.

He feels the US edition's success is helped by having "fresh eyes" on the format and the show having "so much social media presence", which makes it "highly engaging".

Stats given to Newsbeat by TikTok - which called Love Island "one of the most influential entertainment franchises" on the app - suggest he's not wrong.

During the latest series, the hashtag #LoveIsland was mentioned in 123,000 posts in the UK, with #LoveIslandUK featuring in 88,000.

While in the US, #LoveIsland appeared in 1.09m posts and #LoveIslandUSA was tagged in 502,000 posts.

That said, the US population is nearly five times the size of the UK's.

US entertainment journalist Carly Thomas says executive producers have told her they look for ways to "bring in the US audience", be that through social media, challenges and the islanders they choose.

"I think for the US audience, we love to just relate and connect with people," Thomas, who works for The Hollywood Reporter, says.

She also feels the US edition wants to "push the limits" of the islanders with intense challenges and viewers "love to see how far they'll go", including rapper Megan Thee Stallion hosting one which saw them sit on cakes and throw them at each other.

Love Island USA has not been all smooth sailing, though.

Contestants in last year's series faced relentless online bullying which forced the show to broadcast a statement saying it does not tolerate "cyberbullying, harassment or hate". The show insists it takes duty of care seriously.

The US version runs for six weeks once a year, while the UK summer edition typically airs across eight weeks.

There is also now an additional series in the UK throughout the year, with a winter edition airing in 2020 and 2023, which has now been succeeded by All Stars.

The finale of the third All Stars version, which sees ex-islanders return to the villa, attracted about 910,000 viewers earlier this year.

During the most recent UK series, producers tried to get hearts racing, and TikTok numbers up, by introducing some new twists.

A few islanders were summoned for a sleepover at a different villa before Casa Amor, and for the first time, only three couples were in the final after two pairs got dramatically dumped.

Some fans have appreciated the changes, while others, like Sarel, feel they didn't land.

Love Island superfan Dami Amoo, who has watched every episode of the UK, US and All Star editions, says the UK series is starting to feel "overproduced".

"I do think it's been on a steady decline because they're trying to give us what we want, but then they're overdoing it and then they're taking away the classic [elements]."

She thinks this may have been due to budget constraints, but missed the islanders going on exciting dates and taking part in "fun activities or games" where you see their personalities more.

Amoo, 28, also thinks you can really see the impact of investment in the US version, which was aired almost simultaneously with the latest UK edition.

"They've invested so much into the props, the games and all of these brands are part of the actual production," she says.

"Whereas the UK version, it seems like they're just on an island somewhere just doing it on their own.

"You don't get a lot of hype, we don't get British celebrities contributing to the discussions."

The US edition has been able to bring in revenue by becoming a major space for advertising, external, with numerous content partners and more than 1,000 media partners, according to Peacock.

Evans isn't surprised by the US version capitalising on brand partnerships, saying "everything's bigger, everything's brighter, everything's just very American".

So as the sun sets on another run of Love Island series, what could UK producers do ahead of the next launch?

Superfan Dami thinks "they should really get some real fans in the production room".

"The people that do the debriefs online, people who engage on Twitter, they should get us in a room and we tell them what we really, really want."

An ITV spokesperson told Newsbeat "reaction of the fans is at the heart of the show as seen in public votes and including opinions as part of the challenges".

They added Love Island UK "continues to wield huge cultural relevance, both in the UK and in the USA" and to date it has had "over 2bn streams on ITVX and remains the biggest 16-34 show in commercial television".

Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Srosh Khan and Jack Gray.

EntertainmentTab.title: The Sopranos star Vincent Pastore dies aged 80
EntertainmentTab.text:
US actor Vincent Pastore, who played Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero in the hit show The Sopranos, has died aged 80, according to several US outlets.

Pastore was found at his home in the Bronx, New York City and there was no indication of criminality, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.

In The Sopranos, Pastore played Tony Soprano's best friend who ultimately became an informant for the FBI. His character's death in series two was one of the show's most memorable storylines.

Robert Attermann, Pastore's manager, told CBS News: "To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable 'Big Pussy,' but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more."

"He loved being an actor. He was passionate about his craft and was always encouraging, respectful, and generous with young actors, taking the time to offer guidance and support whenever he could," Attermann said.

He continued: "For me, losing Vinny is deeply personal. Over more than three decades, I had the honor of watching not only his remarkable career but also the incredible person he was. I will miss his friendship, his loyalty, his humor, and his heart."

Pastore was born in the Bronx in 1946. He enlisted in the US Navy during the Vietnam War before embarking on a career in acting.

His early credits included roles in movies such as Goodfellas and Carlito's Way.

Later TV appearances included Law & Order, General Hospital and Hawaii Five-O.

But it was his role in The Sopranos which brought Pastore widespread recognition. He appeared in all six seasons of the critically acclaimed show, despite his character being killed off in the second series.

In 2000, Pastore and his fellow The Sopranos cast members won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

EntertainmentTab.title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
EntertainmentTab.text:
It's a song that has become inescapable, whether you're scrolling on TikTok, listening to the radio or even filling up your trolley on the weekly shop.

And now Rein Me In, the melodic love song by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, has officially broken the longest standing record in British music history.

Speaking to Jack Saunders on BBC Radio 1's Official Chart show on Friday afternoon, Fender said he was "speechless" when asked how it felt to break the record.

By spending 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chart, it overtakes the record set by American crooner Frankie Laine with his track I Believe, in 1953.

This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean.

"[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".

He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".

When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".

It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.

Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".

A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.

Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.

It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".

The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".

Ben Mortimer, who runs Fender's label Polydor, described it as a "historic achievement" from "two homegrown stars" - Newcastle's Fender and London's Dean.

In an interview with Radio 1 when the track first hit number one, Fender acknowledged the track's slow climb to the top, thanking "the internet".

He also says he found it interesting that the track "travelled online and people came to it later, which is wonderful really because it's the music that's doing the talking".

The song has become a mainstay on TikTok - a quick scroll through the social media app shows its use on everything from grand declarations of love to montages of holidays and even compilations of football goals and celebrations.

It's also notable that the song first went viral after the pair performed it at a show at the London Stadium, home of Dean's team West Ham, in June last year.

She then returned the favour a week later at Newcastle United's St James Park, performing the song this time at the home of Fender's footballing love.

Whilst TikTok streams do not count towards the official charts, BBC research from last year explored how much of an effect the platform was having on what we listened to, particularly songs with meaningful and powerful lyrics.

EntertainmentTab.title: EastEnders star Shane Richie facing drink-drive charge
EntertainmentTab.text:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.

Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the Church Langley Way area of Harlow, shortly before 23:20 BST on Wednesday.

A force spokesman confirmed the 62-year-old, of Tadworth, Surrey, was arrested and a charge of drink-driving had been authorised against him.

It added Richie, real name Shane Roche, was due to appear at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 9 September.

Richie plays Alfie Moon in EastEnders, making his first appearance in the BBC soap in 2002.

The Sun reported he was arrested, external at a Tesco petrol station forecourt.

Essex Police said: "Officers were called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the area of Church Langley Way, Harlow, shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July.

"On arrival, officers arrested a man.

"A charge of drink-driving has subsequently been authorised against Shane Roche, 62, of Tadworth, Surrey."

Richie's representative has been contacted for comment.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘A reminder of why we have unions’: Matewan writer and director on the film’s lessons for the labor movement
EntertainmentTab.text:
When John Sayles, a student at Williams College taking time off from his summer factory job, was hitchhiking during the summer of 1970 in West Virginia, it was often coalminers who picked him off the main interstate highways.

At the time, miners were amid the wake of a contentious union election within the United Mine Workers of America. Fierce tensions had led to the murder of the union reform candidate Joseph Yablonski and his wife in December 1969.

Miners told Sayles the conflict was comparable to the Matewan Massacre, an event in 1920 he had never heard about before and, like much labor history, had largely been shelved away from the forefront of the American consciousness.

Learning that bit of American history would eventually inspire Sayles to write a screenplay and direct the 1987 film Matewan.

The film, starring Chris Cooper, James Earl Jones and Mary McDonnell, depicts union organizing among coalminers and the efforts of Baldwin-Felts detective agents, hired by the Stone Mountain coal company, to stop them.

In an interview with the Guardian, Sayles noted workers at the coalmine were segregated into groups based on race and ethnicity, a labor tactic referred to as a judicious mixture meant to prevent unionization from occurring.

Yet local West Virginian, Black and Italian-immigrant miners still banded together to strike against the coal company.

“When they went on strike, all three of those groups got together and went out together, and that was really interesting to me, the way that a common enemy can overcome these other prejudices that the miners had,” Sayles said.

The Baldwin-Felts agents, in turn, assaulted, threatened, intimidated and even killed a miner in an attempt to shut down the union effort. A shootout between the two groups on 19 May 1920 would leave seven agents, the Matewan mayor and two miners dead.

The story “was structured like a western. It ends literally with the good guys and the bad guys facing each other on Main Street at high noon,” he said, adding that it had “that kind of strong ending that was kind of perfect to make a film”.

Sayles and several cast and crew of the film, including producer Maggie Renzi and actors David Strathairn, Chris Cooper, Gordon Clapp and Joe Grifasi, appeared at a July reunion screening of the film in Williamstown, Massachusetts.

At the screening, Sayles and Renzi noted the film was made to resurrect a piece of labor history that was at risk of being forgotten.

“I just felt like people needed a reminder of why we have unions,” Sayles told the Guardian about why he made the film. “Without them, you don’t have anywhere to stand.”

Sayles notes that even after the massacre, union organizing at Matewan failed and organizing workers faced significant violent resistance, until the landmark National Labor Relations Act was passed under Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1935 that enshrined collective bargaining rights in the US.

But workers continue to face challenges. Unionizing some industries has become even more difficult because employers can now move workplaces abroad, drastically limiting the power a union has if the work can be done anywhere else, Sayles said, citing ongoing cases of employers who shut down locations where workers were on a path to unionization, such as Walmart and Starbucks.

He also emphasized workers in the US were still hampered by federal laws that restricts organizing, like the Taft Hartley Act of 1947, which prohibits national and sympathy strikes. For example, while strikes in the film industry occur, each craft is separated by its own labor union and must strike independently from one another.

But collective action can bring together large coalitions that inflict change.

EntertainmentTab.title: BTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boom
EntertainmentTab.text:
BTS’s “Army” fanbase is descending on New York this weekend as the K-pop supergroup continues their first world tour after a four-year hiatus, sparking an economic boom wherever they land.

After shows in South Korea and Europe, the group are back in North America, with 14 shows in six US cities in August and September.

Following the rollout of BTS’s sixth album, Arirang, in March, fans have proved they are willing to spend. In Las Vegas, concertgoers who attended four sold-out shows in May generated an estimated $340m in economic activity, with events at huge hotels on the strip and at tiny Chinatown cafes.

HYBE, the group’s label, has partnered with local businesses and cultural centers for the “BTS The City – Arirang” project in select cities, offering exclusive BTS programming for concertgoers.

Ahead of two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on 1 and 2 August, fans can follow a map of activities, landmarks and eateries that celebrate the group.

Manhattan’s Koreatown is bracing for thousands of fans. The economic impact of BTS concertgoers is expected to match that of soccer fans who crowded MetLife Stadium for the World Cup final – which included a BTS performance – a few weeks ago.

BTS will “easily compare [to] or even exceed Fifa’s economic impact just on average spending”, said Michael Mariano, head of economic development at Tourism Economics.

The group’s return has been a boon for HYBE, which reported a record-high revenue of $993m this past quarter.

The Korean Cultural Center New York will serve as the hub for fan activities. Participants who nabbed a coveted reservation can try on K-beauty products, sample desserts from Tous les Jours, a South Korean bakery chain, and customize the light sticks they’ll bring to the concert, known as “Army bombs”.

“K-pop can serve as a gateway to learning the Korean language and discovering Korean beauty, food, technology, tourism and other aspects of Korean culture,” said Bora Yoon, visual arts manager at the center.

The Arte Museum, which houses large-scale digital art, is hosting a special BTS exhibit that will feature music and digital art celebrating the group’s music. The museum expects a high demand for the exhibit, which will immerse BTS fans in “all five senses”, said Sang Jin Lee, head of the creative team and vice-president of d’strict, a creative design company that owns the Arte Museum.

“It’s about sharing our culture, great heritage and Korean contemporary digital art through the lens of BTS, using an enduring folk song that is continually reinterpreted by every generation,” Lee said in Korean, referring to Arirang, the centuries-old folk song that inspired the name of BTS’s new album.

New Wonjo, the oldest Korean barbecue restaurant in New York, is also featured on the map, and plans to serve a special menu inspired by the members of BTS and the foods they miss most on tour, including kimchi fried rice, pork belly and jajangmyeon, or black bean noodles.

The menu was developed “with intention, and is rooted in Korean culture, rather than just pasting ‘BTS’ on a regular menu item”, said Jacob Baik, art director of New Wonjo. “We hope that some guests who might initially visit because of the ‘BTS The City’ project leave with a genuine interest in the restaurant, the food and Korean culture more broadly.”

The map also features bingsu, a type of South Korean shaved ice dessert, offered by Seoul Bingsu – a pop-up version of Seoul-based Tokyo Bingsu, known for its tomato flavor of the dessert. For its limited 10-day New York run, Seoul Bingsu will offer special bookmarks, pins and stickers for those who order from its special Arirang menu.

Ara Go, the Seoul-based owner of Seoul Bingsu, said BTS “has truly helped introduce Korean culture to the world”.

“Food and desserts are a huge part of Korean culture, and I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to promote not only our food but our country with a broader audience,” Go said in Korean.

Before the spot’s collaboration with BTS, Angela May, 18, had never heard of bingsu. May, a BTS fan for nearly six years, traveled to Manhattan from New Jersey to try it.

“Just having BTS written on the menu or the window will bring a lot of attention to the place,” May said.

Asli Penaeo, 22, grew up in New York and has been a fan for seven years, yet she has never been to most of the collaborating restaurants.

“This event is finally giving me a chance to go to some of these restaurants, try new items, but also make new memories with fellow Army [fans],” she said, sipping on a BTS-branded Tous Les Jours strawberry lemonade.

Sunmi Lee, 40, an interior designer, said she was considering taking a BTS-themed double-decker bus tour to visit New York landmarks – even though she lives in the city.

“It’s about celebrating Korean culture,” she said. “Trying authentic local spots, and feeling connected to something bigger than just a concert.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverage
EntertainmentTab.text:
ABC has pushed back aggressively against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for putting the network under an expedited license renewal process for eight local television stations it owns, charging in a lengthy filing that the process is payback for the network’s editorial decision-making and coverage of Donald Trump.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: Accommodate the administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” lawyers representing the Disney-owned network wrote in a 109-page filing, submitted as a reply to petitions from conservative media groups to deny ABC’s licenses. “The tools vary; the objective does not: a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely.”

The FCC chair, Brendan Carr, has denied that inquiries into the network relate to its editorial decision-making and instead said they stem from concerns about the company’s employment practices and compliance with statutory obligations.

ABC’s lawyers pointed out how unusual it is for the FCC to demand that a group of network-owned stations apply several years early to renew their licenses. Other ABC-owned stations have licenses that run all the way until 2031.

“The commission’s departure from those norms lays bare what is really going on: the administration is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights,” ABC’s lawyers wrote. “Because this whole proceeding rests on an unconstitutional premise, the stations should never have been asked to justify license renewal years early.”

Responding to petitions to deny ABC’s licenses based on accusations of liberal bias, the network’s lawyers pointed out that the “commission has no authority to regulate the content of television programming”.

“No Petitioner has established any ‘violations’ of Commission rules or regulations, let alone the ‘serious’ ones or the ‘pattern of abuse’ required to warrant denying renewal,” they added.

ABC’s lawyers also argued that its eight stations had made “essential contributions to their local communities” in markets such as New York City and Philadelphia and argued that the FCC should dismiss the petitions to deny their licenses.

Participants have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny. After that time, the FCC could choose to either grant the license renewal requests – an unlikely prospect – or schedule hearings on the matter, beginning a potentially onerous and time-consuming process that could run for several years, particularly if an adverse ruling is challenged in the courts.

On Tuesday, a bipartisan coalition of former FCC commissioners and staffers submitted a filing urging the commission to reject the petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals, arguing that the early renewal process ordered by Carr’s FCC in April is “a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution”.

Thousands of commenters have filed on behalf of ABC in both the license renewal inquiry and another FCC investigation into the daytime talkshow The View for a potential violation of rules guarding political candidate appearances.

“When given the chance to weigh in on whether to allow the FCC to continue its campaign of censorship and control, the American public showed up in a big way, and the vast majority who spoke up delivered the same message,” Anna M Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement on Thursday. “They believe in the value of their local news, they trust those who cover their communities, and they understand that the FCC has no business deciding who is a journalist and what counts as real news.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands
EntertainmentTab.text:
Jack Bessant, bass

We were hanging out with the lovely producer George Drakoulias at Abbey Road. He said, “We’re going to bring in some instruments for you guys” – and replaced the fairly low-budget ones we’d been playing. I was given this beautiful 1960s Fender Jazz bass.

Sometimes you pick up an instrument you’ve never touched before and immediately start playing stuff you wouldn’t normally play. It made me want to come up with something cool, James Jamerson-style, with that Motown feel. I found the riff that became the bassline to Place Your Hands, showed it to Gaz, and he came up with this chilled melody about going down by the water. When Kenwyn House, our guitarist, added that classic opening guitar riff, it changed from something mellow into something much more action-packed.

It was just a lovely time to be alive. We were young and everyone in the band was talented, even though we didn’t really know what we were doing. We were rockers at heart, but we were very open-minded. We listened to everything from Motown and Bob Marley to Van Morrison’s Common One – Summertime in England can still make me cry. I eventually bought an old Telecaster bass – you can definitely hear the reggae influence in the bass during the bridge to Place Your Hands.

I’ve always thought the emotion Gaz brought to it was incredible, but I didn’t fully understand what he was singing about until quite recently. He explained that “put your hands on” was a metaphor for wanting a hug, to help him through the grief of losing his grandfather. I hadn’t realised at the time because we were young rockers, swept up in the moment and full of testosterone, with no time to think about anything. The 90s wasn’t really a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive – there were all the lads’ mags, and we were playing that game to an extent. We certainly didn’t discuss our feelings in the way we would now. Looking back, I think the lyrics are beautiful.

I don’t think we’ll ever get bored of playing it because it’s so funky and full of rhythm and spirit. We’ve had quite a few lineup changes, and Place Your Hands is the song that has always pulled us together. It gets people dancing and putting their hands up – even though the lyric is actually “Put your hands on”.

Gary Stringer, vocals

We were signed to S2 in 1993, under the legendary figures Lincoln Elias and Muff Winwood. Our first album reached the Top 10, we had three Top 40 singles and played Glastonbury, so we were really happy. We were touring the west coast of the US with stoner-rock band Kyuss when Lincoln suggested we meet George Drakoulias, who had worked with Rick Rubin at Def Jam and helped discover the Beastie Boys. George turned up wearing flowing white robes, which made quite an impression, and we decided to go with him for the second album.

We recorded three or four songs at Abbey Road. George hired a 1960s Fender bass. Jack was fiddling around with it and started playing what would become the bassline to Place Your Hands. Kenwyn dropped his guitar’s E string down to D and came up with the riff that sits over Jack’s bassline. At first, I sang it quite gently, but then thought: “That’s too airy-fairy.” We went to Los Angeles to finish the album with George, taking the bassline and guitar riff with us.

The lyrics are about the death of my grandfather, Kenneth. I was on the tour bus when I got a call saying he had died. I went to the morgue and my auntie said: “Do you want to see Ken?” I’d seen a dead body beside the road while on a surfing trip in Morocco when I was 18, but this had a different impact. The lyrics are essentially asking for comfort – for a cuddle. That’s why it’s “Put your hands on”. I’m sure if it was “Put your hands up” the song would have been even bigger.

Chris Evans was a huge supporter of the band and played the single to death on Radio 1. When you went on TFI Friday, it didn’t matter if you were Dave Grohl or Oasis – you had to do the It’s Your Letters segment and sing those words to the melody of the song you were on the show promoting. For some reason, our version of It’s Your Letters stuck. “Put your hands on” and “It’s your letters” have the same number of syllables, so they used it every week ever after.

The video cost about £250,000. We were turning head over heels on wires that had to be threaded through holes cut into our trousers. Place Your Hands accounts for a lot of my income. If we had 10 songs like that, I’d be a multimillionaire.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Trumpeters? We think we’re the kings of the orchestra’: Wynton Marsalis prepares to blow the Edinburgh festival away
EntertainmentTab.text:
At Heinz Hall in Pittsburgh, Wynton Marsalis is hard to spot. When he first played this venue, in 1984, he was the prodigious 22-year-old soloist out front, blowing Haydn’s trumpet concerto under the baton of Lorin Maazel. Tonight he is embedded in the machinery: half-hidden behind ranks of strings and woodwind, a black-suited figure in the heart of his own symphony.

It’s a strange way for a composer to behave – especially one whose public persona has long been associated with certainty, polemic and the upright authority of a man who can make any argument sound like a moral law. Yet Marsalis seems almost pleased by his disappearance. “It’s my piece,” he says, as we talk in his hotel room the next morning, “but it’s not my show.”

The piece is All Rise, Marsalis’s first symphony, written in 1999 – a mammoth hybrid for a 15-piece jazz band, a 50-piece orchestra and a 100-piece choir, premiered at the turn of the millennium by the New York Philharmonic with Kurt Masur. Across 12 movements, Marsalis paints a sprawling civic canvas whose building blocks are American – marches, blues, dance rhythms – and whose aspiration is almost embarrassingly large: to sound like pluralism.

This year’s Edinburgh international festival has built its artistic theme around the piece: on the opening night at Usher Hall, Marsalis and his Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra will join the Royal Scottish National Orchestra and massed choirs. That’s more than 200 performers in total. Edinburgh has had no shortage of big opening statements over the decades, but this is a particularly pointed choice: a work first conceived as a celebration of integration, now revived in a moment when the very idea of common culture has begun to look quaint.

In the past, Marsalis could be confrontational: a man with a rulebook and a relish for battle. Today he’s mellower: quick to credit others, reject ego and talk more about collaboration than correction. He’s keen to puncture the myth that a symphonic work is the solitary utterance of genius. “All Rise was a collaborative exercise. James Oliverio, a soundtrack writer, was teaching me how to orchestrate while I was doing it. I had Milan Turković, the great Austrian bassoonist, helping me with the woodwind. But the main man was the late conductor Kurt Masur. He was always goading me to write something for him. ‘Are you afraid to write for the New York Philharmonic?’ he’d say. Kurt saw a segregated New York, and wanted a piece that brought people together.”

Masur – East German, Beethovenian, exacting – was conscripted into the German army as a teen in the final months of the second world war. “I remember he told me then, ‘You think that nazism is unique to Germany? It can happen here.’ Kurt said nazism didn’t happen because people were poor: it happened because lots of Germans wanted to behave like that. And, coming from the south, I could relate to that.”

For some, All Rise is exhilarating: a large-scale attempt to make American music sound like an argument worth having. For others, it feels like an impossible negotiation: two institutions – orchestra and big band – asked to behave like one. Marsalis has always been furiously outspoken about what he sees as the malign role of “fusion” in jazz, and is equally wary of the limits of fusing jazz and symphonic music. “I wanted to draw from American mythology and find intersections. Because with some music, there is no common ground.”

For instance? “You’re not going to hear a jazz version of a Beethoven symphony. It’s too many chord changes.” Marsalis’s first symphony is instead built on the dance music shared by Americans. “It’s about the relationship between tango and choro; between ragtime and Anglo-Celtic fiddle music; between New Orleans marches and European band counterpoint. But you have to be aware of certain things. In classical music, the basses don’t play all the time. In our music, it plays all the time. And in classical music, the percussion is accent, but in jazz and Latin music, it’s everything.

“So you have to find the common ground that you intersect with. Because if you’re not on that ground, there’s no intersection. John Coltrane said he was looking for a universal coefficient. It’s like the word mama. You say mama, it has a universal sound and feeling to it.”

He talks a lot about seeking links with other musics – about what he’s learned from the Iraqi oud virtuoso Naseer Shamma, Ghanaian percussionist Yacub Addy, Irish-American violinist Mark O’Connor, and about his enduring friendships with Willie Nelson and Paul Simon. “I meet up with Paul as much as I can – we talk a lot about the relationships between African-American and Anglo-Celtic music, how that is the foundation of pretty much everything we all do.”

Unlike some of Marsalis’s other large-scale pieces, All Rise is not a polemic. “If you want to know how I think jazz can help democracy, listen to [2020 album] The Ever Fonky Lowdown. If you want to hear what I say about government corruption – and how our government has always been corrupt – listen to my song Super Capitalism, on [the 2007 album] From the Plantation to the Penitentiary. But All Rise is different, it’s about bringing people together.”

Drawing from spirituals, gospel music and European devotional sources, All Rise is also full of God. Has his faith changed since writing it? “No. I always had a very strong spiritual faith that was not denominational, even as a kid. I came from very spiritual people. I spent a lot of time with my great uncle, who was born in 1883. He was a stonecutter for the cemetery. If you are around death that much, you become religious.

“But I never believed in the dogma. I always noticed the contradictions in Christianity: the saviour was poor, the church is rich. The saviour took a vow of poverty and said, ‘Love people.’ But a lot of religious people don’t love people who aren’t into their religion. So my libretto constantly counterstates that. I draw from the Muslim call to prayer as much as the Bible.”

Marsalis, now 64, is fascinated by such ecumenical statements: he remembers his father telling him to read Autobiography of a Yogi when he left high school. “That book was hard work. My dad told me to carry a notebook and write down the name of each swami. When you want to make connections, you have to really work at it.”

One connection he’s worked at is his marriage. Marsalis recently married Scottish violinist Nicola Benedetti, who also happens to be director of the Edinburgh international festival. They have a daughter, Elise, born in May 2024. Their relationship is largely long-distance at the moment – lengthy FaceTime chats and phone conversations. Would he ever move to the UK? “I’m going to have to plead the fifth on that one, I’m afraid,” he says with a chuckle, but also dismisses the prospect of Benedetti joining him in New York. “She’s not going to do that,” he says with a resigned smile.

Benedetti, 26 years Marsalis’s junior, has been a frequent collaborator. “What really made me fall in love with Nicola was when I wrote a violin concerto for her,” says Marsalis. “After the first run-through, she sent me a list of about 40 notes. First I laughed. Then I read them. And each of them were tiny things she thought I should change. Her detail was quite incredible. ‘If you put the violas on beat one of the 58th bar, that will save us 20 minutes of rehearsal time. Maybe put the bassoon’s entry at the end of bar 112, on the four of the bar rather than the two. Maybe stress the first beat of that passage in 5/8 time.’ And so on.

“I was amazed that she was able to notice all of this while playing the piece. I have so much respect for her, the time she spends practising, her dedication to the humility of study, the desire to learn, to get better. And she is completely collegiate in the way she deals with ensembles.” Has he learned humility from her? “Maybe. Trumpeters, we think we’re the kings of the orchestra, there to blow down the walls of Jericho. We think the piece only starts when we start playing. We know the strings are doing something but we can’t figure out what the hell they’re up to. Maybe I’m less like that now …”

I suggest that people will already expect young Elise, with such parentage, to grow up as a virtuoso musician. “She’s a hell of a singer,” he says. “But you can’t determine what your children do. I’ve got three sons – only one is a musician. He’s mainly a visual artist, but he makes music as part of his practice. One teaches track and soccer. Another teaches literature. I never put them in any direction – I just wanted to make sure they have integrity.”

How is he coping with late fatherhood? “You know, I always used to hang out with older people. All my mentors were older men – not just my father, but Clark Terry, Dizzy Gillespie, Sweets Edison, Elvin Jones, August Wilson, Romare Bearden, Ralph Ellison. And, when you’re hanging out with old people, you stay 19 for ever. But I’ve always enjoyed hanging with young people too. It’s a privilege when people come up after gigs, teenage kids with their parents, asking for advice. It takes a village to raise a child. We’re all raising the same kid.”

When Marsalis began running the jazz orchestra and jazz programme at Lincoln Center – New York’s pre-eminent arts complex – he was just 26. “I was one of the youngest in the orchestra, alongside legends who had worked with Ellington and Basie. Now I’m probably the oldest.” He recently announced that he will be stepping back from his executive leadership role after nearly four decades, while remaining involved artistically for a transition period.

It’s easy to imagine Marsalis as an Alex Ferguson-type spectral presence, presiding warily over anyone who takes up the reins. “No, I’m not going to be like that. There are so many talented people in the band now who could carry on what I’m doing. The bassist Carlos Henriquez, the alto saxophonist Sherman Irby, tenor saxophonist and clarinetist Dan Block – all amazing professionals. But it’s not my choice: there’s a whole executive board at the Lincoln Center who will be making that decision.”

Maybe stepping away from the Lincoln Center has altered his angle of vision. For decades it was his pulpit for declarations; now he sounds more interested in how musicians learn one another’s language – happy to defer, amused by his own ego. “I think about Copernicus and Galileo, about how they both observed that the Earth was not the centre of the solar system. They realised that, every time you discovered a new body, the equation became more complicated, until you stopped clinging to the old ways of looking at the universe. Maybe we all need to do that.”
